scores.why: Arc: Sil's frame ends on a held cut end she will not let go of, so the story closes on its own image. Register is mostly spare and concrete, and the tide, tally, plumb-line and cut-end stops are strong. Weaker stops (the Ram in the Surf, the Ebb Hound) lean on sentiment more than the others. Most stops earn their place.

Arc: Hesk's counting gives a shape and the closing cut end offers a faint hope, but the middle sags. The Bailer and The Fid are flat, and The Gull That Stays overlaps The Gull Who Waited. The Counting Hands and Lantern Boat are good, but several stops could be cut without loss. Register is solid, with some pleasing lines like 'a count left unfinished is a debt.'

The second-person grandmother voice is the closest match to the bible's tone, and the cliff-walk frame is well conceived. But the arc is diffuse across sixteen stops, and several (the Name-Kite, Widow's Shawl, Lamp Kite, Tallow Lamp) repeat material from other epics with little new. Varuk sits too close to Varo and the Varosk hound, which muddies the cast. The ending on the Tally Kite is fitting but the count-as-lesson line is a little explicit.

Aun's first-person confession has a complete arc: the tailless kite a boy learns from, the cut he cannot take back, the open question at the end, 'I am still holding the knife.' The voice is spare and self-accusing, which fits the bible's dry, tender register. Stops like the Unstitched Gull, the Upturned Hull and the Sun-Kite's Ribbon carry real weight, and each one tightens the guilt. Very little is wasted.

The gull's-eye hopping structure is distinctive and each stop is a concrete object, which fits the register well. The Gull Who Lost a Word, the Boat That Turned Back and the Tethered Gull are among the best stops in the set. The Water Bag is a tonal outlier that works as dry humour but reads lighter than the rest. The ending on an open question is deliberate, but it gives less closure than the strongest epics, and several stops are reused from other tellings.

Structure is the strongest of the set: it opens at the Spindle, travels the Lamp Road, and ends in the Unflown on the line 'A cut, she says, is only half a sentence,' which gives the arc a real last word. Stops such as the Knot Belt, the Bride-Kite, the Parted String and the Water Bag (with its dry sting) are concrete and earn their place. The Loom Weight and Sun-Kite's Ribbon repeat other tellings, but the sequence as a whole reads as a designed telling rather than a list.
